body_text:
Every rational number has a decimal expansion that either
terminates (has only finitely many nonzero fractional digits) or
is eventually periodic. Conversely, every eventually periodic
decimal expansion represents a rational number.

This dichotomy follows from the division algorithm: when dividing
integer $a$ by nonzero integer $b$, each step produces a remainder
in $\{0, 1, \dots, |b|-1\}$. By the Pigeonhole Principle, after at
most $|b|$ division steps, either a remainder of $0$ is reached
(yielding a terminating expansion) or a previously seen remainder
recurs, forcing all subsequent quotient digits to repeat in a
cycle of length at most $|b|-1$. Conversely, an eventually
periodic expansion can be summed via a geometric series into a
closed-form ratio of integers.
